title: The scholar who turned to bhakti
hookLine: a young renunciant faints in a temple, a scholar carries him home to teach him, and the lesson turns around
carry: bhakti: where learning finds its goal in love
tomorrow: a renunciant asks a governor to teach him. why keep saying 'more'?

lines: A STRANGER FAINTS IN THE TEMPLE.
cards: Plenty of Hindu families have two camps: the ones who read the texts, and the ones who sing. Today's scene puts them in one room.
A young renunciant walks into the temple of Jagannatha at Puri, sees the image, and drops to the floor, senseless. People stare. One man steps in: Sarvabhauma, a learned teacher of Vedanta.
He has the stranger carried to his own house. The stranger is Chaitanya. And the scholar is about to give him lessons.

teach.b: In the Charitamrita's telling, Sarvabhauma is kind, and a little protective of this young monk.

He teaches him the Vedanta sutras, the dense threads that sum up the Upanishads, day after day, and Chaitanya sits and listens without a word. At last the scholar asks: are you understanding any of this?
The answer is gentle and blunt at once. I understand the sutras, Chaitanya says. It's your explanation I can't follow.
Their meaning is clear, like the sun; the commentary covers it, like a cloud. Then he gives his own reading.

Brahman, the ultimate reality the sutras are about, isn't only a formless truth to be known, he says in the book's telling; it's Bhagavan, God with a form and a name, and the goal of all that study is bhakti, love.
The book says the great scholar turned to devotion. That's a big Hindu teaching in one scene.
There's a path of knowledge, jnana, and a path of love, bhakti, and for Chaitanya's followers, knowledge finds its goal in love. Fairly told: this is the Charitamrita's story.

Shankara's followers read the same sutras through his commentary, and many walk the path of knowledge with deep devotion of their own. And look at how it happens. Chaitanya doesn't win the first exchange.
He listens for days. So if your family has a reader and a singer, this story says they aren't on different paths for long.

teach.h: LEARNING FINDS ITS GOAL IN LOVE.
teach.b: A fitting close to a week of patient teachings, and of a love God longs to feel from our side.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas tell the story of Sarvabhauma at Puri as a turn from dry learning to devotion and sing kirtan as that devotion; Advaita Vedantins continue to read the sutras through Shankara's commentary.

o: a study of the sutras with no feeling
devotion as the goal of learning
a debate won by quoting the most texts

games.q: the scholar and the stranger — tap the pairs.
p: a Vedanta teacher who took him home
the sutras' meaning, and the commentary over it
the path of knowledge, the path of love

s: in the story, Chaitanya corrects Sarvabhauma on the first day
he sits and listens, day after day, before he says a word.
Chaitanya says the sutras are clear like the sun, and the commentary covers them like a cloud
then he gives his own reading, with devotion at the center.
the story settles which school of Vedanta is right
it's the Charitamrita's story; Shankara's followers still read the sutras through his commentary.

games.q: at a family puja, your uncle says kirtan is for people who can't read the texts, and real Hinduism is philosophy. by the Charitamrita's story, what's a fair reply?
o: in that story, the great scholar of the sutras turned to bhakti. knowing and loving can meet.
he's right. bhakti is only for people who don't study.
the texts don't matter in Hinduism. only feeling counts.
games.why: Sarvabhauma knew the sutras as well as anyone in Puri, and the book says he turned to bhakti. for Chaitanya's followers, learning finds its goal in love; Shankara's followers walk the path of knowledge, many with deep devotion too.

practice: If you know a bhajan or a kirtan, play one softly, or hum a single line, and simply listen to it for the whole sit. If you don't, listen to one sound near you: a fan, traffic, your own breath.
When the mind starts explaining or preparing a reply, as minds do, come back to listening.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti: devotion. In this scene, it's where a great scholar's learning finds its goal.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Bengali bhakti, devotion; in this story, what Chaitanya places at the center of the sutras' meaning.

carryVoice: Carry this from the scholar at Puri: bhakti, where learning finds its goal in love. That's the week.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya-lila 6 (Chaitanya faints at the sight of Jagannatha; Sarvabhauma has him carried home; the Vedanta lessons, Chaitanya's silence, the sun-and-cloud reply; Chaitanya's reading of Brahman as Bhagavan, with bhakti as the goal; Sarvabhauma's change)
